paras: The killing of Howell and pursuit of Jim Newton took place in December 1888 in Stevens County, Kansas, when a farmer named Howell was reported beaten and shot to death by Jim Newton, described as a notorious horse thief, and a posse of farmers set out after Newton. Several versions of the wire story said the posse meant to lynch Newton, but no report of his capture appears in the coverage.

According to the Omaha Bee's Topeka correspondent, Newton had been stealing horses in the southwestern counties and running them across the Indian Territory line, where he would be safe from the law. Another version said he "hails from Beer City, in the neutral strip."

On Friday night, December 14, Howell heard a noise in his barnyard and found Newton preparing to leave with three of his best horses. When Howell ordered him to release the horses, Newton was said to have fired a pistol; Howell attacked him unarmed, was beaten about the head, and was then shot, three times in most versions and twice in one. Newton rode off into the Territory with the horses.

Howell's body was found the next day or the day after; the dispatches variously say Saturday, Sunday, and "this morning" under a December 17 dateline. A posse of farmers was organized and followed Newton. The shorter Topeka wire said the posse started after him "bent upon lynching him," and the Omaha Bee reported "great excitement" and predicted he would be lynched if found.

No report of Newton's capture, a lynching, an inquest, or a trial was found in the coverage. A dispatch from Nevada, Missouri, dated December 19 quoted Judge C. T. Davis, a former prosecutor, who said Newton had once stolen cattle in Bates County, escaped from a Linn County, Kansas, jail by knocking out his jailer with a stool leg, and later served a penitentiary term.

The story spread as a Topeka dispatch from December 17, carried in Washington, Annapolis, Alexandria, Clarksville, Memphis and Wheeling and in weeklies in Kansas, Michigan, Wisconsin, Dakota, Iowa and Ohio through December 27. Headlines such as "Murdered by a Horse Thief" and "Killed by an Outlaw" cast Newton as a "desperado" and Howell as a "plucky" farmer protecting his property. The papers mentioned the posse's lynching aim without comment, and the Kansas paper's version did not mention lynching at all.

No paper gave a race for either man. The Wheeling Register's one-line summary placed Howell in Indian Territory, and the Butler Weekly Times put the killing in "Newton county," but nearly every other version named Stevens County.

reader.title: Killing of Howell and pursuit of Jim Newton
bases: After the farmer Howell was found shot, a posse of farmers pursued Jim Newton, and some wire versions said it was 'bent upon lynching him' or that he would 'undoubtedly be lynched' if found (A1, A3, A5); no capture or lynching is reported, so this is at most a threatened lynching (A2, A12).

No report in the coverage says Newton was caught or killed; the papers report only a posse of farmers in pursuit, with lynching intent stated in some versions (A1, A3, A12). Howell's own death was a homicide attributed to one man, not to a group (A2).

The killing of Howell and the posse's pursuit appear in several independent wire versions (a Topeka Associated-style dispatch, a special telegram to the Omaha Bee, and a Missouri dispatch), though the lynching intent appears in only some (A1, A2, A3, A15).

accounts.label: Topeka wire (short version)
accounts.gist: Newton beat the unarmed Howell senseless and shot him; the body was found Saturday and a posse started after Newton 'bent upon lynching him.'

accounts.label: Topeka wire (long version)
accounts.gist: Howell ordered Newton to release the horses, Newton fired a pistol, beat and shot Howell; a posse of farmers was organized and is following him, with no lynching intent mentioned.

accounts.label: Omaha Bee special telegram
accounts.gist: Same events, adding that Newton planned to run horses across the line out of reach of the law and that if found he 'will undoubtedly be lynched.'

accounts.label: Nevada, Mo., dispatch
accounts.gist: A former prosecutor recounted Newton's past cattle theft, jail escapes and penitentiary term.

framing.detail: Papers ran the Topeka dispatch under heads such as 'Murdered by a Horse Thief' and 'Killed by an Outlaw,' presenting the theft and killing as fact and the posse's lynching aim without comment.
The Butler Weekly Times headed its follow-up 'Jim Newton's Record' and called him 'the notorious desperado, horse thief and murderer.'
